extracted.intended_audience: users of the Singular computer algebra system; graduate students, researchers, and practitioners in computational algebra, algebraic geometry, singularity theory, integer programming, and coding theory
extracted.subtask_description: Reference material describing monomial/module/matrix/product orderings, standard bases and related algebraic invariants, algorithms for toric ideals and integer programming, Gauss–Manin/spectrum computations, and decoding with Groebner bases as implemented in Singular.

rubrics_metrics.name: reverse lexicographical ordering (ds)
rubrics_metrics.description: let deg(x^α) = α1 + · · · + αn, then x^α < x^β ⇔ deg(x^α) > deg(x^β) or deg(x^α) = deg(x^β) and ∃ 1 ≤ i ≤ n : αn = βn, . . . , αi+1 = βi+1, αi > βi.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a global/local ordering in Singular (denoted ds). Example usages appear in ring declarations. This ordering prioritizes total degree, then reverse lexicographic tie-break.

rubrics_metrics.name: negative degree lexicographical ordering (dp)
rubrics_metrics.description: let deg(x^α) = α1 + · · · + αn, then x^α < x^β ⇔ deg(x^α) > deg(x^β) or deg(x^α) = deg(x^β) and ∃ 1 ≤ i ≤ n : α1 = β1, . . . , αi−1 = βi−1, αi < βi.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Denoted dp in Singular (negative degree lex). Prioritizes total degree, then lexicographic with opposite comparison on components; useful for local orderings.

rubrics_metrics.name: weighted reverse lexicographical ordering (ws)
rubrics_metrics.description: ws(w1, ..., wn), w1 a nonzero integer, w2, ..., wn any integer, is defined as ds but with deg(x^α) = w1α1 + · · · + wnαn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generalizes reverse-degree-lex by using integer weight vector to compute degrees. Can produce custom graded orderings; combine with other orderings for complex needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: weighted lexicographical ordering (Ws)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ws(w1, ..., wn), w1 a nonzero integer, w2, ..., wn any integer, is defined as Ds but with deg(x^α) = w1α1 + · · · + wnαn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weighted lexicographic version; use when lexicographic tie-break with weighted degrees is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: module ordering giving priority to coefficients ((<,C) and (<,c))
rubrics_metrics.description: (<,C): x^α e_i <_m x^β e_j ⇔ x^α < x^β or (x^α = x^β and i < j). (<,c): x^α e_i <_m x^β e_j ⇔ x^α < x^β or (x^α = x^β and i > j).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These module orderings prioritize the polynomial monomial part (coefficients) before the component index. Examples show how Singular prints vectors (as sums of coeff*gen(i)) under such orderings.

rubrics_metrics.name: module ordering giving priority to components ((C,<) and (c,<))
rubrics_metrics.description: (C,<): x^α e_i <_m x^β e_j ⇔ i < j or (i = j and x^α < x^β). (c,<): x^α e_i <_m x^β e_j ⇔ i > j or (i = j and x^α < x^β).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These module orderings prioritize the component index over the polynomial monomial. Under orderings starting with 'c' Singular writes vectors in bracketed component form [v1,...,vr]. Examples illustrate different printed orders.

rubrics_metrics.name: M-ordering (matrix ordering)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let M be an invertible (n×n)-matrix with integer coefficients and M1,...,Mn the rows of M. The M-ordering < is defined: x^a < x^b ⇔ ∃ 1 ≤ i ≤ n : M1 a = M1 b, ..., M_{i−1} a = M_{i−1} b and M_i a < M_i b.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Matrix orderings encode lexicographic comparison of the transformed exponent vectors M a vs M b. Singular accepts integer matrices; warns if matrix is not n×n or not full rank (may cause non-termination or nonsensical results). Matrix orderings are more expensive than built-in global/local/block orderings.

rubrics_metrics.name: product (block) orderings
rubrics_metrics.description: Given ordered variable sets x and y with monomial orderings <1 on K[x] and <2 on K[y], the product ordering (<1, <2) on K[x,y] is: x^a y^b < x^A y^B ⇔ x^a <1 x^A or (x^a = x^A and y^b <2 y^B).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Singular allows arbitrary combinations of global, local, matrix orderings into product orderings; e.g., lp on first 3 variables, matrix ordering on next 3, ds on next 4, ws on last 3. Use to create block-structured term orders.

rubrics_metrics.name: extra weight vector (a(w1,...,wn))
rubrics_metrics.description: a(w1,...,wn) defines deg(x^α) = w1α1 + · · · + wnαn and enforces deg(x^α) < deg(x^β) ⇒ x^α < x^β and deg(x^α) > deg(x^β) ⇒ x^α > x^β.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An extra weight vector does not define a monomial ordering by itself; it can only be combined with other orderings to insert an extra line of weights into the ordering matrix. Example ring declarations show combinations like (a(1,2,3),wp(4,5,2)).

rubrics_metrics.name: pseudo ordering L (max exponent)
rubrics_metrics.description: L(max exponent) is not an ordering but sets the maximal allowed exponent for polynomials in this ring. The default is 32767; reflected in attribute 'maxExp'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to restrict exponent sizes in a ring. Affects ringlist and ring construction from lists. Useful to avoid runaway exponents.

rubrics_metrics.name: standard basis (Groebner-like) of a submodule
rubrics_metrics.description: For R = Loc<K[x]> and submodule I ⊆ R^r, denote L(I) the submodule generated by leading terms. f1,...,fs ∈ I is a standard basis if L(f1),...,L(fs) generate L(I). A standard basis is minimal if ∀i: (f1,..,fi−1,fi+1,..,fs) ≠ I. A minimal standard basis is completely reduced if ∀i: reduce(fi,(others)) = fi.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This generalizes Groebner bases to modules. The manual gives definitions and examples; 'completely reduced' is a strong canonicality condition achieved by reduction of each element w.r.t. the others.

rubrics_metrics.name: normal form (NF) properties
rubrics_metrics.description: A function NF : R^r × {G | G a standard basis} → R^r, (p,G) ↦ NF(p|G), is called a normal form if for any p ∈ R^r and any standard basis G: if NF(p|G) = 0 then L(g) does not divide L(NF(p|G)) for all g ∈ G.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NF(p|G) is called a normal form of p w.r.t. G. The function may also be applied to any generating set, but result may not be unique. NF is used for reductions and membership testing.

rubrics_metrics.name: ideal membership via normal form
rubrics_metrics.description: For a standard basis G of I the following holds: f ∈ I if and only if NF(f, G) = 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical criterion: reduce f modulo G; zero normal form ⇔ f in ideal. This is the standard Groebner-basis membership test generalized to modules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hilbert function and Hilbert–Poincaré series
rubrics_metrics.description: For a graded module M over K[x1,..,xn] with weights (w1,..,wn), Hilbert function HM(k) := dim_K M_k. Hilbert–Poincaré series H_P_M(t) := Σ_{i=-∞}^∞ HM(i) t^i. For weights (1,..,1), can be written as Q(t)/(1−t)^n = P(t)/(1−t)^{dim(M)} with Q,P ∈ Z[t].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes first and second Hilbert series and relation to Hilbert polynomial. For quasihomogeneous modules use weighted denominator Π_i (1 − t^{w_i}). Useful to compute dimensions and polynomial growth of graded components.

rubrics_metrics.name: syzygy module and k-th syzygy
rubrics_metrics.description: Given I = (g1,...,gs) ⊆ R^r, the module of syzygies syz(I) is kernel of map R^s → R^r sending Σ w_i e_i ↦ Σ w_i g_i. The k-th syzygy module is defined inductively as syzygies of (k−1)-st syzygy module.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Syzygy modules depend on choice of generators but are unique up to direct summands. Singular can compute syzygies (example output provided).

rubrics_metrics.name: free resolution and Hilbert Syzygy bound
rubrics_metrics.description: A free resolution of M = R^r/I is ... → F2 →^A2 F1 →^A1 F0 → M → 0, where columns of A1 generate I. Resolutions need not be finite; Hilbert Syzygy Theorem: for R = Loc<K[x]> there exists a (minimal) resolution of length ≤ number of variables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Singular can compute minimal resolutions (mres) and print matrices A1,A2,... Examples illustrate construction and printing of matrices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Betti numbers and regularity
rubrics_metrics.description: For graded ring R and graded submodule I ⊂ R^r, with minimal free resolution given, the graded Betti number b_{i,j} is minimal number of generators e_{a,j} in degree i+j of the j-th syzygy module. Regularity of I is smallest integer s such that deg(e_{a,j}) ≤ s + j − 1 for all j.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Singular provides betti(resI) and regularity(resI) to compute Betti table and Castelnuovo-Mumford regularity. Examples show interpretation of output.

rubrics_metrics.name: triangular sets, characteristic sets, and irreducible characteristic series
rubrics_metrics.description: Let < be lex order with x1<...<xn. For f∈R, lvar(f) is largest variable, ini(f) its initial coefficient in that variable. A set T={f1,...,fr} is triangular if lvar(f1)<...<lvar(fr). (T,U) is a triangular system if ini(T) does not vanish on V(T)\V(U). T is irreducible if certain pseudoremainder and prem conditions hold. For G={g1,...,gs} there exist irreducible triangular sets T1,...,Tl s.t. V(G)=⋃_i V(Ti\,Ii). Such {Ti} is an irreducible characteristic series of (G).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characteristic decomposition represents variety as union of triangular components; Singular can compute char_series(i) and print components. Useful for solving polynomial systems by triangularization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gauss–Manin connection and spectrum computation
rubrics_metrics.description: For an isolated hypersurface singularity f, the n-th cohomology bundle carries a flat connection with covariant derivative ∂_t. The V-filtration and Hodge filtration on Brieskorn lattice define the singularity spectrum Sp; Sp(α) := dim_C Gr_α^V Gr_F^0 G. Spectral numbers lie in (−1,n) and are symmetric about (n−1)/2. Spectrum is constant under μ-constant deformations and satisfies semicontinuity under small deformations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Singular libraries (gmssing.lib, mondromy.lib, spectrum.lib) can compute monodromy matrices, V-filtration, and spectrum for (non)degenerate principal parts. Examples show commands monodromyB(f), vfilt(f), spectrumnd(f) and interpretation of outputs (spectral numbers, multiplicities, Milnor number, geometric genus). Semicontinuity tests semicont(s1,s2) and semicontsqh(s1,s2) used to bound numbers of singularities on hypersurfaces.

rubrics_metrics.name: use of Singular libraries for spectrum and monodromy
rubrics_metrics.description: LIB 'mondromy.lib'; matrix M = monodromyB(f); LIB 'gmssing.lib'; list l = vfilt(f); commands print(l[1]) for spectral numbers, print(l[2]) for multiplicities, print(l[4]) for monomial basis of H''/s*H'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples demonstrate how to compute and interpret monodromy, V-filtration, spectrum, basis elements, and standard basis of Jacobian ideal. Notes: spectrumnd(f) works only if leading part is nondegenerate; spectrumnd(f,1) can be faster if nondegeneracy is known.

rubrics_metrics.name: definition of toric ideal I_A
rubrics_metrics.description: Given integer matrix A (m×n), for u∈Z^n define u^+,u^- with disjoint support and u=u^+−u^-. For u≥0, x^u denotes monomial. The toric ideal I_A := (x^{u^+} − x^{u^-} | u ∈ ker(A) ∩ Z^n) ⊂ K[x1,...,xn]. Also I_A = I : (x1···xn)^∞ where I = < x^{v_i^+} − x^{v_i^-} | v_i basis of integer kernel >.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Computing finite generating sets requires lattice basis of ker(A) (via LLL) and saturation. Toric ideals link to integer programming and have special combinatorial structure exploited by algorithms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conti–Traverso algorithm for toric ideals
rubrics_metrics.description: Compute I_A via extended matrix B = (I_m | A). Consider ideal I1 = < y^{a_j^+} − x_j y^{a_j^-} | j = 1..n > in K[y,x]. Adjoin t and t·y1···y_m − 1 to get I2 in K[t,y,x]; I2 is saturated. Then eliminate t,y1,...,y_m to obtain I_A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Algorithm requires many auxiliary variables and is slow in practice but important for integer programming applications because it can find initial solutions and verify solvability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pottier algorithm for toric ideals
rubrics_metrics.description: Compute a lattice basis v1,...,vr for ker_Z(A) via LLL. Form I1 = < x^{v_i^+} − x^{v_i^-} | i =1..r >. Saturate by introducing t and t·x1···xn − 1 to get I2 in K[t,x]; eliminate t to obtain I_A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Similar to Conti–Traverso but starts from lattice basis of A; uses one auxiliary variable t and elimination. Simpler than Conti–Traverso in variable requirements but still uses auxiliary variable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hosten–Sturmfels algorithm for toric ideals (no auxiliary vars if condition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assumes A contains a row-space vector w with positive coefficients. Compute lattice basis via LLL; I = < x^{v_i^+} − x^{v_i^-} > is homogeneous w.r.t. positive grading w. Use lemma: for homogeneous ideal w.r.t. weighted reverse lex with weight w and var order x1>...>xn, Groebner basis G of I yields Groebner basis of (I : x_n^∞) by dividing each element of G by highest possible power of x_n. Compute IA = I : (x1···xn)^∞ by successive saturations (I : x_1^∞) : x_2^∞ : ... : x_n^∞, using up to n Groebner computations (can be reduced).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoids auxiliary variables and is practical and fast in many cases; requires existence of positive grading vector w in row space of A (a real restriction). Successive Groebner basis computations are usually easy after the first.

rubrics_metrics.name: Di Biase–Urbanke algorithm for toric ideals (variable flips)
rubrics_metrics.description: Performs up to n/2 Groebner computations, needs no auxiliary variables, but requires existence of a kernel vector without zero components. It finds lattice basis v1,..,vr with v1 having no zero components then flips chosen variable columns to obtain matrix B and lattice basis u1,..,ur meeting positivity assumption, then applies a 'variable flip' elimination procedure to obtain generators of I_A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relies on structural preprocessing (finding v1 with no zero components) and variable sign flips. Useful when its precondition holds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bigatti–La Scala–Robbiano algorithms for toric ideals
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine ideas of Pottier and Hosten–Sturmfels. Use one auxiliary variable u and generator x1···xn − u (instead of t·x1···xn − 1). Authors also propose a parallelization attempt (not implemented in the library).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alternative approach to saturation/elimination; additional technique to eliminate auxiliary variable u is nonstandard. Parallel variant exists in literature but may not be implemented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Buchberger algorithm specializations for toric ideals
rubrics_metrics.description: Toric ideals are prime and generated by binomials, which allows optimizations: describe Buchberger operations via vector additions/subtractions, multiple reduction strategies, and bit-vector support representations for monomials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These structural optimizations (Pottier, multiple reduction, bit-vectors) improve Buchberger performance on toric ideals compared to general ideals.

rubrics_metrics.name: solving integer programming via toric ideals
rubrics_metrics.description: For IP min{c^T x | x ∈ Z^n, Ax=b, x≥0} with c≥0: (1) compute toric ideal I(A); (2) compute reduced Groebner basis G(c) of I(A) w.r.t. monomial ordering refined from c; (3) reduce x^v modulo G(c) for an initial feasible v; if reduction yields x^w then w is optimal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If no initial solution known, extend instance via Conti–Traverso extended matrix to find solvability and an initial solution. The advantage: steps (1) and (2) done once if varying b, making solving many b-instances efficient; classical Branch-and-Bound often faster in single-instance settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: use of LLL for computing lattice basis (toric algorithms)
rubrics_metrics.description: The required lattice basis of ker(A)∩Z^n can be computed using the LLL-algorithm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: LLL is standard preprocessing step in multiple toric-ideal algorithms; the manual references algorithm sections where LLL is used.

rubrics_metrics.name: codes: definitions and decoding concepts
rubrics_metrics.description: A linear code C ⊆ F_q^n, Hamming distance d(x,y)=#{i|x_i≠y_i}, weight wt(x)=#{i|x_i≠0}. Minimum distance d(C)=min_{x≠y∈C} d(x,y). Cyclic codes correspond to ideals in F_q[x]/(x^n−1). Complete decoding: given y find c∈C with minimal distance; bounded decoding unique if d(y,C) ≤ (d(C)−1)/2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sets up notation and structures used in decoding sections. Use polynomial rep for cyclic codes and splitting field with primitive n-th root of unity for syndrome computations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cooper philosophy: generic vs online decoding
rubrics_metrics.description: Generic decoding: precompute closed formulas CF by solving some system S(C), then evaluate at received syndrome to decode. Online decoding: solve system S(C,r) for each received word r. Generic decoding has heavy preprocessing but cheap decoding; online decoding concentrates effort per received word.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choice of strategy depends on application: many decodings of same code favor generic approach; one-off decoding favors online approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: CRHT-syndrome ideal construction for cyclic codes
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce variables and equations to model syndromes and error parameters, forming polynomial system FC ⊂ F_q[X,Z,Y]. The zero-dimensional ideal I_C generated by FC is the CRHT-syndrome ideal associated to code C; its variety V(FC) is the CRHT-syndrome variety (after Chen, Reed, Helleseth, Truong).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modeling decoding as solving zero-dimensional polynomial system allows use of Groebner-basis techniques; properties of solutions correspond to error locations/values.

rubrics_metrics.name: existence and properties of general error-locator polynomial L_C
rubrics_metrics.description: Every cyclic code C possesses a general error-locator polynomial L_C ∈ F_q[X1,...,X_{n−k}, Z] satisfying: L_C = Z^e + a_{t−1} Z^{e−1} + ... + a_0 with a_j ∈ F_q[X_1,...,X_{n−k}], and for syndrome s corresponding to error of weight t ≤ e, evaluating X_u = s_u gives roots of L_C(s,Z) equal to the error location values and 0 with multiplicity e−t.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: L_C is an element of the reduced Groebner basis of the ideal generated by the syndrome system. Having L_C reduces decoding to univariate factorization; computing L_C is central to the Cooper approach and CRHT method.

rubrics_metrics.name: finding minimum distance via polynomial systems JC(w)
rubrics_metrics.description: For binary cyclic code C with defining set S_C, build system J_C(w) (equations summing powers of Z variables and constraints) such that number of solutions of J_C(w) equals w! times number of codewords of weight w. For 1 ≤ w ≤ d, either J_C(w) has no solutions (w<d) or has some (w=d).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This algebraic approach reduces minimum-distance computation to checking solvability of polynomial systems; examples referenced in decodegb library show practical use.

rubrics_metrics.name: generalized Newton identities and error-locator polynomial expansion
rubrics_metrics.description: Error-locator polynomial σ(Z) = ∏_{l=1}^t (Z − z_l) expands as σ(Z) = Z^t + σ_1 Z^{t−1} + ... + σ_t; coefficients relate to power sums and syndromes via generalized Newton relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These identities underpin algebraic decoding via syndrome equations and polynomial relation solving; used in derivation of the equations in CRHT systems and computation of locator polynomials.
